title: The economics of repair
bodyMd:
A manufacturer argued that consumers' frequent replacement of appliances proved they preferred novelty to durability. A repair cooperative disputed the inference. For several popular models, replacement parts were sold only as expensive assemblies, and opening the casing required tools unavailable to most independent repairers. Under those conditions, buying a new appliance might be the cheapest practical response to a minor failure, even for a consumer who valued durability.

The cooperative proposed a trial in which a retailer would offer otherwise comparable appliances with different repair arrangements: one with affordable individual parts and accessible service information, another with the existing restrictions. Purchases alone would not settle the issue, because initial prices and expected repair needs also affect choices. Nevertheless, observing choices with repair costs made explicit would reveal more about consumer preferences than interpreting replacement behaviour under a single constrained set of options.
